Some strands snap one after another and recoil onto the slice or pizza; others remain attached until the slice moves farther away. A soft tacky tearing sound may accompany the pull, against the faint scrape of the crust. Overhead light picks out pale yellow highlights and small oil glints. Avoid perfectly parallel strings, endless stretching, floating toppings or cheese cutting cleanly all at once.

Yeasted dough in a bowl expands over many minutes, not seconds. Its rounded top gradually lifts and spreads toward the sides as trapped gas enlarges tiny pockets inside the soft, elastic mass. The surface stays continuous, with slight dimples and tension around folds; flour dust remains patchy rather than moving independently. In a time-lapse, marks on the bowl make the increasing volume clear. At normal speed the dough is effectively silent, with only a faint tacky sound if someone touches or releases it. Soft kitchen light shows a matte cream surface and gentle shadows. Avoid balloon-fast inflation, pulsing, morphing or dough passing through the bowl.

A piece of meat laid on a hot, lightly oiled pan makes immediate contact along its lowest points. Tiny bubbles form at the edges as surface moisture escapes, producing a steady, irregular sizzle and occasional sharper pops. Over the next minutes, the underside browns where it touches the pan; edges tighten, curl slightly and draw inward as moisture leaves and proteins contract. Small beads of juice appear on top, while a thin sheen of fat moves across the pan. The piece stays anchored by friction until lifted or turned with tongs. Avoid instant uniform browning, dramatic shrinking in a second, hovering meat or sizzling without visible heat and moisture.

In a hot frying pan, oil forms a thin, shimmering film around the food. When a water droplet reaches it, a brief burst sends tiny beads outward in short arcs; they strike the pan, nearby stovetop or splash guard and settle as separate glossy dots. Larger droplets move less far and fall quickly, while the finest spray catches the light for an instant. Sharp, irregular pops sit over the steadier frying hiss. Repeated bursts come from wet patches, not from every part of the pan at once. Avoid floating beads, sparks in place of oil, droplets passing through solid surfaces or a continuous fountain from a dry pan.

In a windowpane, a bright lamp or face can appear twice: one sharp reflection from the near surface and a fainter, slightly offset copy from the far surface. The separation grows when viewed at a steeper angle or through thicker glass. Both copies move together as the camera shifts, while the view beyond the pane remains visible beneath them. Indoor reflections stand out against a dark exterior; in daylight they may nearly disappear. The pane itself makes no sound, so keep only the room or street ambience. Do not make the copies drift independently, float in front of the window, or appear equally bright.

Through a curved drinking glass or bottle, straight background lines bend toward its edges, and objects may appear wider, narrower, or briefly inverted depending on the vessel’s shape and contents. As the camera moves sideways, the distorted image slides across the glass faster than the background; highlights travel along the curved surface. Thick rims and bases create stronger warping than thin walls. Clear glass has faint grey-green edges and small white reflections. It makes no sound unless handled, when it gives a light clink. Keep the distortion confined to the glass silhouette; do not warp the surrounding scene or make objects pass through the vessel.

A straight straw leaning through a glass of water appears kinked at the waterline. The submerged section looks shifted sideways and sometimes slightly wider because light bends when it passes between water, glass, and air. From a fixed viewpoint, the kink stays exactly at the visible water surface, not halfway down the straw. Moving the camera changes the apparent offset; moving the straw makes both sections move together. The waterline curves gently upward against the glass, with small ripples after a touch and a soft tap if the straw meets the rim. Do not physically bend the straw or let its lower section slide independently.

In low, direct sunlight, fine sprinkler droplets can show a rainbow to someone looking toward the spray with the sun behind them. The coloured arc sits against the mist, with red on its outer edge and violet toward its inner edge; it appears strongest against dark trees or shade. As the sprinkler head turns, individual droplets fall in short curved paths and sparkle, while the visible arc brightens or fades where dense mist crosses the viewing angle. The spray makes a steady hiss and patter, with a faint mechanical click from some rotating heads. Do not attach painted colour bands to the water stream or show the rainbow from every camera position.

Sunlight passing through a rippling pool surface makes thin, bright, shifting lines on the floor, steps, and swimmers below. The lines meet in irregular loops and flare briefly where small surface waves focus the light; darker blue-green gaps remain between them. Their motion follows the waves but is not locked to any one ripple: patterns stretch, split, and reconnect continuously. They bend across a person’s skin or a tiled step without leaving those surfaces. Hear water lapping, splashes, and the muffled pool ambience, not a sound from the light itself. Avoid static grid patterns, glowing lines in midair, or highlights that pass through opaque objects.

Under a leafy tree in direct sun, patches of light and shadow cover the ground, walls, and people. Small gaps in the canopy cast soft-edged bright spots, often rounder than the leaf shapes; closer leaves cast clearer silhouettes. A breeze makes branches sway with a slight delay, so the patches drift, overlap, narrow, and reopen rather than flashing randomly. Leaves backlit by the sun look translucent green, with darker veins and occasional bright edges. The sound is leaf rustle, birds, and nearby ambience; sunlight itself is silent. Do not make the light patches float off the surfaces or move without corresponding movement in the foliage.

At night, neon signs and illuminated shopfronts stretch into broken coloured reflections across wet asphalt. Shallow puddles can show a recognizable inverted sign; rough pavement breaks it into short red, blue, or green streaks aligned with the viewing angle. As a car passes, tyres push water aside and ripples briefly bend the reflected letters. People and kerbs interrupt the reflections, while raised dry patches stay comparatively dark. Streetlights add pale highlights and the sky usually remains darker than the signs. Hear tyre hiss, dripping water, footsteps, and traffic. Avoid a perfectly mirrored road, colours glowing without a source, or reflections sliding independently of the water.

At night, oncoming headlights appear as two bright points at a fixed spacing, growing larger and brighter as the vehicle approaches. The lit road and nearby objects brighten too; on a damp road, each lamp may leave a long broken reflection. In a camera, intense light can produce a soft halo, limited lens streaks, or a small ghost image that moves when the camera angle changes. Haze makes the beams visible as broad cones, while clear air usually does not. Hear the approaching engine and tyre noise, rising then fading after the car passes. Avoid glare that covers unrelated parts of the frame or headlights that move separately from the vehicle.

A bright sun, headlight or bare bulb can scatter light inside a camera lens. The image may show a soft veil around the source, small coloured ghost shapes along a line through the frame centre, or a streak from an anamorphic lens. As the camera tilts, these shapes shift in relation to the light source; they do not stick to a building or a person. Flare can briefly lower contrast and wash out nearby detail, especially at sunset. It makes no sound of its own: keep the street or room audio unchanged. Avoid decorative rainbows without a bright source, and avoid identical flare on every shot.

During a fast pan, a passing motorcycle or a quick arm movement, blur follows the direction of movement during the camera’s exposure. A fast object leaves a short, continuous smear of its own colours while still keeping a readable leading edge; a longer exposure makes the smear wider. When the camera tracks the object, it can stay relatively sharp while the background streaks sideways. Blur changes from frame to frame as speed changes, and stops when movement stops. The matching sound follows the real action: an engine passes and recedes, or fabric swishes. Avoid doubled limbs, crisp frozen wheels beside heavily blurred surroundings, and objects smearing through solid obstacles.

Many digital sensors record the frame line by line rather than all at once. During a rapid pan, vertical poles can lean slightly in the same direction; a fast rotating fan can look bent. For ordinary handheld footage, keep these effects subtle: walls, faces and parked cars should retain stable shapes. A sudden camera jolt may cause a brief wobble that settles with the movement, not a permanent wave across the picture. The sensor effect has no sound; any accompanying noise comes from the camera handling or the scene. Avoid rubbery buildings, faces that stretch between frames, and objects morphing or sliding independently of the camera.

Depth of field is a gradual change in sharpness around the focused distance, not a cutout around a subject. If a camera focuses on a person’s eyes, their ears may be a little softer, people several metres behind them softer still, and distant streetlights may become rounded highlights. A nearby hand reaching toward the lens can go out of focus before the face does. As focus shifts, sharpness moves smoothly through the space; objects do not change size or position. Focus itself is silent, apart from any faint camera motor noise. Avoid uniformly blurred backgrounds, razor-sharp hair edges against blur, and foreground objects that stay sharp at every distance.

A crowd has uneven spacing. Friends and families form small clusters; gaps open around a cart, doorway or seated person, while a narrow entrance brings shoulders closer together. From a high angle, heads vary in height and size with distance. People slow before a bottleneck, take short steps, adjust their paths and resume speed when space opens. Clothing moves with each stride, and bags swing slightly behind the body’s motion. Voices overlap into a soft, changing murmur, with footsteps and occasional nearby calls distinct. Avoid evenly gridded people, duplicate faces, bodies passing through one another, and a packed group moving at identical speed.

Background people have their own small purposes rather than performing for the camera. On a pavement, one person checks a phone while walking, another pauses at a shop window, and two others talk as they continue past. Their pace differs; someone waiting shifts weight between feet or turns toward an approaching companion. Farther figures appear smaller and less detailed, and they disappear behind parked cars or doorframes before reappearing. Footsteps, snippets of conversation and rustling clothing mix into the location sound without every voice becoming clear. Avoid synchronized head turns, repeated gesture loops, people staring at the lens, and figures sliding without foot contact.

On a busy Baghdad street, compact cars, taxis, SUVs, minibuses and occasional motorcycles share the road. Vehicle spacing varies: a queue compresses near a junction, then opens as cars accelerate. Drivers edge forward at low speed, brake visibly before stopping, and steer around a parked vehicle without passing through its mirrors. Tyres remain on the road; bodies dip slightly under braking and rise as speed steadies. Sunlight flashes across windscreens, while dust softens distant contrasts. Engines idle and rev, horns sound briefly, and tyre noise changes with speed. Avoid identical cars in perfect lanes, synchronized starts, silent traffic, and vehicles sliding sideways without turning their wheels.

At a street crossing, pedestrians look toward approaching traffic, judge an opening and step off the kerb at different moments. One person may walk steadily while another briefly slows beside a family member; neither teleports into the road. Feet plant in alternating steps, weight passes over each foot, and a carried bag lags and swings as the walker changes pace. Drivers approaching the crossing slow before reaching people, leaving visible space. Footsteps become clearer near the camera, mixed with engines and street voices. Avoid everyone starting together, walkers gliding without steps, people passing through vehicles, and cars stopping instantly without a braking distance.

At a bakery counter or ticket window, people stand in a loose line facing the service point, usually about an arm’s length apart. The front person steps away after being served; the next person advances, followed by small, delayed steps farther back. Feet lift and settle rather than sliding, bags swing briefly, and shoulders turn to make room. Someone may check a phone or speak to a companion without losing their place. Shoes scuff the floor beneath low conversation and the counter worker’s voice. Keep each person’s position and clothing recognizable as the camera angle changes; do not let people float through one another.

In a busy Iraqi market lane, shoppers move in both directions between stalls, slowing near displays of produce, fabric, or household goods. Small gaps open and close as people turn their shoulders, pause, or step sideways to pass. A person carrying bags needs more clearance; the bags swing after each change of direction. Vendors remain near their counters while customers gather in short, shifting clusters. Footsteps, bargaining voices, rustling bags, and an occasional cart wheel blend together. Sunlight from the open lane meets softer shade beneath awnings. Keep bodies grounded and routes continuous, without people sliding sideways or passing through stalls.

A blue ceramic cup placed beside a brass tray should remain the same cup in every frame and camera angle. Its handle stays on the same side relative to the cup, its rim keeps its shape, and its position changes only if a hand touches and moves it. When lifted, the cup rises with the hand, briefly tilts with the wrist, and makes a light ceramic tap when set down. Its shadow shifts with the light and its new position. In a home or café scene, nearby keys, chairs, and plates follow the same rule: no popping into view, duplication, morphing, or passing through the tabletop.

topic: consistent number of fingers and limbs
body: A visible human hand has a thumb and four fingers attached to one palm, with joints that bend in consistent directions. When a person lifts a tea glass, the fingers close around it, some becoming hidden behind the glass rather than vanishing; they reappear in the correct positions when the hand turns. Arms connect naturally at shoulders and elbows, while legs remain attached at the hips as a person walks. Sleeves fold at bending joints, and footsteps sound when shoes meet the ground. In close shots of customers talking or paying, avoid extra fingers, fused hands, duplicated arms, or limbs that switch sides between frames.

topic: text on signs staying the same
body: A shop sign’s Arabic or English lettering stays identical across wide shots, close-ups, and camera movement. Each letter keeps its order, spacing, colour, and position on the sign; perspective may make the text narrower at an angle, but it must not change the wording. Painted letters follow the wall’s flat surface, while raised plastic letters cast small shadows and do not drift separately. If a person crosses in front, the person briefly hides the text, which appears unchanged afterward. Street voices and traffic continue beneath the shot; a loose metal sign may rattle in wind. Avoid invented letters or text that flickers between frames.

A logo printed on a paper cup, delivery bag, or shopfront keeps the same symbol, colours, lettering, and proportions in every shot. On a curved cup, the print wraps around the surface and narrows toward its edges; on a swinging bag, it moves with the bag and may crease where the material folds. A glossy sign catches highlights, while matte ink stays comparatively flat. Paper rustles, a bag handle creaks, and nearby café or street sounds remain natural. When a hand covers part of the mark, the hidden portion does not change. Avoid mirrored logos, drifting prints, altered spelling, or a new design after a cut.

A person’s outfit keeps the same garments, colours, patterns, and accessories across cuts. A cream shirt remains tucked or untucked as established; its collar, buttons, and sleeve length do not change when the camera moves. Walking makes fabric sway and form folds at elbows, knees, and the waist, with heavier denim moving less than a light scarf. A shoulder bag stays on the same shoulder unless the person visibly shifts it. Cloth gives a faint rustle beneath footsteps and conversation. In a family gathering or market scene, track each person separately, avoiding swapped outfits, disappearing jewellery, changing patterns, or sleeves that morph through the hands.

Light should retain a believable source and direction across shots of the same moment. In a room with daylight entering from a window on the left, faces, furniture, and wall textures remain brighter on that side; shadows fall consistently to the right, even when the camera reverses angle. A warm ceiling bulb adds a softer amber pool beneath it. People crossing the window briefly interrupt the light, while moving curtains make gentle changes in brightness. Room conversation, footsteps, and a faint fan hum continue naturally. Do not let daylight jump to another window, shadows flip without cause, or skin and clothing change colour between cuts.
